prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength, opening the 10^-18 regime of atomic timekeeping

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B035 alone, Katori and Ye. Having read the full exchange I am more, not less, confident in it, but for reasons that differ from the ones I gave before. The chair asks what physical step makes the lattice clock distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. My answer is that the magic-wavelength condition is a genuine concept: it lets the trapping potential be made irrelevant to the clock transition, so that a large ensemble can sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime and be interrogated in parallel. That trades the single-ion route's limit on signal-to-noise against its freedom from perturbations, and it is a different route to the same accuracy, not a refinement of Wineland's. It also opened a new set of physics questions (collective and many-body shifts, density and lattice-light effects) that Ye's group then had to control to reach about 1e-18. The record is reproduced and compared across JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, so there is no live dispute about what was measured. On the second chair question, I would have the citation rest on the invention and the realisation, with 1e-18 as the demonstrated consequence, since that wording answers the overlap objection and fits the idea-plus-realisation split between Katori and Ye. I treat the pending redefinition of the second as supporting, not necessary: the clocks already test constancy of constants and resolve gravitational redshift at millimetre scales, and that stands without a metrology vote. Finally, on opening-ballot breadth, I regard it as a prompt to test the case, not as evidence of merit, and the test has held.
statement.case_against: The reservation I cannot remove is that this is an achievement of measurement and technique, and a sceptical colleague can read it as the third prize in a single line of precision spectroscopy after 2005 and 2012. I think the overlap objection fails on the physics, but I accept that it is a judgement and that Eriksson, Olsson and Johansson are right to want it stated explicitly in the record. A two-name prize also leaves out Lemonde, Takamoto, Lisdat and the Yb and PTB groups, and no wording of the citation fully expresses that; I accept this as the ordinary cost of the three-person limit and not a defect specific to this case. Finally, B008 remains in my view the more far-reaching idea, and I would not like it recorded that I preferred the clocks because they are easier to attribute and not because I judge the science sufficient.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B035 and adds B023 for Halzen alone, as a two-part prize pairing a precision-measurement invention with an observational discovery in astroparticle physics, and flags the one-name credit as an attribution compromise.
responses.response: I do not support the second part, and I would rather say why than leave it as silence. The diffuse flux is well established and the instrument achievement is real, but the claim we would be crediting is a discovery whose meaning is still partial, with the origin of most of the flux unresolved. More importantly, a one-name credit for a collaboration-scale detector is not a principled attribution: you name Karle and Spiering as outside it and say you cannot verify the division of roles. B035 does not need a companion to be complete, and adding one only to use a third seat would let the weaker attribution dilute the clean one. I would be open to IceCube in a later year, once source identification is firmer and the credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering is better documented, but not as a shared prize now.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B008 on conceptual breadth and speed of experimental test, but says he would not defend it against a well-argued shift to B035 because of the HgTe credit, and asks that support for B008 not depend on skipping the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang question.
responses.response: We agree on the substance, and I do not want to skip the conversation you ask for. The reason I do not put B008 first is exactly the one you give: the citation would have to rest on the prediction of the Z2 effect and its first observation, and the HgTe proposal that connects the two sits outside the three names, with Zhang no longer living and the three-dimensional work outside the set as well. I still think the idea is bigger than a clock. But a prize is a statement about who did what, and Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are a partial statement. On your own point about unfamiliarity with the clock field, the question I would ask is the one you ask: what is new? The many-atom magic-wavelength lattice is the answer, and I think it is a stronger reply than the objection to it. If the committee found a way to word B008 so that it did not mislead about the HgTe step, I would move it to second place, which is why I keep it as the first alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B006 to B035, says the lattice-clock idea is distinct from the single-ion clock, asks that the citation say 'invention and realization' and not claim every clock result, and still weighs the Higgs discovery higher in pure scientific significance.
responses.response: I agree with the citation wording and with your reasoning that the trapping and interrogation of a large atom ensemble is a different physical concept from a single-ion clock; we reach the same place. On the Higgs, I do not dispute its significance, and I would not claim the clocks are the larger result. But I would not put B006 ahead for the reason you and Eriksson give: any three names from ATLAS and CMS are a proxy for thousands, and the committee has no principled rule for choosing among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee. Where I am less sure than you is on the gravity argument; a millimetre-scale redshift measurement is a striking demonstration, but I would not lean on it in the citation, because it is a consequence of the clock's accuracy rather than the invention itself.

responses.point: Kroll argues that neither the 2005 comb prize nor the 2012 ion-control prize covers neutral-atom lattice clocks, and asks whether Ye's credit is for the lattice clock specifically or a wider programme.
responses.response: I agree that the field has not been over-rewarded, and I would answer your attribution question narrowly: Ye's credit should be for bringing the lattice clock to the accuracy frontier and for showing that collective effects can be controlled, not for the comb work or cold-matter programme in general, which the 2005 prize already covers. That is the point at which the citation avoids duplicating earlier prizes. I would add one caution to your 'sharply defined invention' framing: the magic-wavelength idea is clean, but the realisation required a great deal of work by several groups, and we should say in our own record that the two names stand for the idea and the leading realisation, not for the whole community.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice as a distinct invention from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I judge it is, but this is a judgement the committee must make explicitly.
Whether two names fairly represent the Sr and Yb groups (Lemonde, Takamoto, Lisdat, PTB, SYRTE) that contributed to the 10^-18 record.
Whether the committee would prefer to wait for the redefinition of the second; I treat it as supporting, not necessary.
Whether B008 could be worded to deal with the HgTe proposal and the 3D work within three names; as it stands I think not.
I rely on general knowledge for accuracy records and priority history, and have not verified them from the supplied material.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My documented ties (Max Planck institutes, Oxford, Freiburg, Gothenburg) and co-authors do not include any credited name on the shortlist, and my research in turbulence, statistical physics and neural networks is not the field of any candidate. I have noted the disclosures by Johansson, Olsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce and see no need for any recusal on my own account.
